prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-achievement prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. After the full exchange the case rests on three points that survived the criticism. First, the idea is specific and attributable: trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that the clock transition is not shifted by the lattice removes the old trade-off between atom number and systematic uncertainty, which is a conceptual step and not only better engineering. Second, the claim is mature in the sense that matters for a prize: the performance has been reproduced and intercompared by several independent laboratories, and no member has raised a doubt about reproducibility. Third, the two roles are distinct and traceable, concept and the demonstration of record accuracy and stability, so two names follow the structure of the achievement. On the chair's scope question, I would frame the prize as an invention that created a new measurement regime and not as general precision spectroscopy: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize covered control of single quantum systems and ion clocks, whereas the lattice clock interrogates a large ensemble of neutral atoms with the motional shifts engineered away, which is a different route to the same precision. The citation should say so and should not claim the field. Having read the exchange I have not moved to B022, which is secure as a phenomenon but still has an open pairing mechanism, nor to any other candidate.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining reservation is category: the immediate achievement is a measurement capability, and its largest consequences (a redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, limits on constant drift and dark-matter searches) are still mostly prospective. A committee that weights new phenomena above new instruments would reasonably prefer B022, and I do not claim the clock is uniquely correct, only that it is the most mature and cleanly attributed. The second reservation is credit at the margin: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Sterr, Gill and others contributed to early strontium lattice demonstrations and to the stability record, and a two-name prize cannot represent them; the citation wording is the only mitigation. Third, overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a matter of degree and must be argued explicitly, not assumed away.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B022) is a discovery of a new phenomenon, preceded by a seven-year-old theoretical prediction and widely reproduced, whereas the lattice clock is a capability whose payoff is still prospective, and he argues that Bistritzer must be named.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-capability criterion seriously and I think his prediction-then-experiment point is the best argument for B022. I still reach a different conclusion for this year for two reasons. The statutes speak of discovery or invention, and the clock is an invention that changed what can be measured, as other precedents for measurement inventions show. And the maturity of the interpretation differs: the superconducting pairing mechanism and the phase diagram of twisted bilayer graphene remain debated, whereas the clock's performance is a quantitative result confirmed across laboratories. On his Bistritzer point I agree with him: if B022 comes forward the 2011 two-author paper cannot fairly be credited to MacDonald alone, and the experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero is the real difficulty. That is why I keep B022 as my first alternative and see the disagreement as one of timing.

responses.point: Lindroth, the other atomic physicist on the committee, asks that the citation be worded around the magic-wavelength lattice clock itself and that the committee acknowledge Lemonde and the SYRTE group and the ion-clock lineage; she also stressed that the clocks feed back into fundamental physics.
responses.response: I accept her wording constraint and have changed my citation to name the invention of the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level, with no broader claim about precision spectroscopy. I agree the committee should record in its deliberation that Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the Sterr and Gill groups contributed to the early demonstrations and the stability record. I do not think that obliges a third name: Katori's concept is the origin, and the record accuracy and stability programme is traceable to Ye, so the two-name credit does not misstate who did what. On her point that the clocks feed back into fundamental physics, I agree, but I would keep it out of the citation because those results are still largely to come.

responses.point: The chair asked whether Ye's role is best described as an accuracy and many-body programme or as a distinct invention, and rejected pairing the clock with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (B037) in a shared prize because it would dilute the clock and break the three-person limit.
responses.response: On B037 he is right and I withdraw any suggestion of a combined prize: the two share optical lattices but are different achievements, and a shared citation would need four names. I keep B037 only as a distant alternative. On Ye's role, I would describe it as the realisation of the lattice clock at record accuracy and stability together with the systematic-shift control that made 10^-18 credible, which is closer to demonstrating the invention at its limit than to a second, separate invention. That is why the citation puts invention and realisation together and names Katori for the concept. I would not word Ye's role as many-body physics, since that part of the programme is less settled and not needed to carry the prize.

responses.point: Olsson proposes verifying the 10^-18 uncertainty figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks against primary intercomparisons before the citation is fixed, and wants the citation to name the concept and its realisation without claiming the whole field.
responses.response: I agree on both. I flagged in round 1 that my 10^-18 figures were recalled, and I would not let the committee fix numerical wording from memory. The citation I now propose therefore states the level only as approximately 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, and the staff should confirm the figures and the order of the first demonstrations before the vote. I note this is a check on wording and not on the scientific claim: independent intercomparisons are described by every member who addressed it, and none of us has stated a doubt that would change the ranking. I also agree that her own B008 should not be pressed given her stated closeness to that field.

uncertainties: The 10^-18 uncertainty figures and the chronology of the first strontium lattice demonstrations are from recollection and should be checked against primary intercomparisons before the citation is fixed.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct advance from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, or reads it as an extension of them.
How much weight Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Sterr, Gill and Hinkley should carry against the two-name credit.

Whether the committee prefers a new phenomenon (B022) to a measurement capability when both are available, and whether the unsettled pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene should be disqualifying.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period; Hall's group is part of the lineage of precision laser spectroscopy and frequency metrology near this work, but my profile records no direct collaboration, joint publication or institutional tie to Katori or Ye, and I judge this to be field proximity that does not require recusal on B025. I also participated in WACQT management, which is near B016, and my quantum-memory and cold-atom-adjacent work is near B037; neither candidate is in my preferred configuration, and I will leave B016 discussion to those without that proximity if the committee prefers. I flag all of this for the committee to judge and will abide by its decision.
